title: Reliability of quantum communication over erasure channels
problem: An erasure channel loses each transmitted system with probability \(p\) and tells the receiver which ones were lost. Its quantum capacity, \(1-2p\) logical systems per channel use, has been known since 1997. Capacity says only that the error can be made to vanish at lower rates, not how fast. The reliability function is the best exponential rate at which it vanishes with the number of channel uses. What is it, and do stabilizer codes with Clifford encoding and syndrome correction reach it, or do general quantum encoders do better?
result: For systems of prime dimension \(d\) and \(0<p<\tfrac12\), the reliability function is found exactly at every positive rate \(r<1-2p\) that is at least the critical rate \(r_{\rm crit}=[1-(d^2+1)p]/[1+(d^2-1)p]\). There it equals the binary relative entropy of \((1-r)/2\) with respect to \(p\), in natural logarithms, and stabilizer codes with syndrome correction attain it. For \(p\ge1/(d^2+1)\) this covers every positive rate below capacity. The same expression is an upper bound at all rates for arbitrary encoders and decoders, and the paper gives random-coding and expurgated lower bounds below the critical rate.
significance: Exact error exponents are scarce in quantum information, even for simple channels. This one holds against all quantum encoders and decoders, so it shows that Clifford encoding and syndrome measurement lose nothing in exponent in the stated range. The formula has a plain reading: errors are dominated by the channel erasing more than the fraction \((1-r)/2\), at which the rate would exceed capacity, and the exponent is the probability cost of that event. Erasures with known positions are a realistic model for atom loss and for leakage that is detected.
limitations: Below the critical rate, which is positive for \(p<1/(d^2+1)\), the bounds do not meet, and the paper shows that its combined lower bound stays strictly below the upper bound. Stabilizer arguments use prime \(d\). The model assumes independent erasures, perfectly known positions and noiseless surviving systems. The statements are asymptotic, about exponents and not finite-length constants. The lower-bound techniques specialize earlier random-coding and expurgation methods, and at sufficiently high rates the same exponent was already known for guessing the physical error of stabilizer codes; the new part is the converse for arbitrary encoders and the resulting match. The authors state that OpenAI "GPT-6 Astra" was used to explore proof strategies and to support the writing.
summary_basis: Description based on the arXiv HTML of v1, read 2026-11-23: Secs. 1–2 (including the optimal-recovery theorem), Sec. 3 up to the change-of-measure proposition, the numerical illustrations and the conclusion; Appendices A and B were not read in detail. Editorial checks: the closed form of the random-coding exponent agrees with direct minimisation of Eq. (77) for five parameter sets; it equals the converse at (d, p, r) = (2, 0.1, 0.5), (2, 0.2, 0.05), (2, 0.25, 0.1) and (3, 0.05, 0.7), and falls below it at (2, 0.1, 0.3), 0.22284 against 0.22694. The critical rates 0.9223, 0.3846 and 0 for d = 2 reproduce. For the five-qubit code the logical ambiguity is 0 for up to two erasures and 2 for three or more, and a(E) + a(complement of E) = 2 for all 32 patterns.
methods_basis: Based on the linked paper version. Derivations marked as editorial, and suggested uses in other problems, are editorial guidance rather than results of the paper.
description: The task is to send one half of a maximally entangled state on \(k\) logical systems through \(n\) uses of the channel, with no prior entanglement, no feedback and no side communication. The error is one minus the overlap of the recovered state with the target. At a fixed rate \(r\), the best error decays like \(e^{-nE(r)}\), and \(E(r)\) is the reliability function. The paper defines it for all encoders and decoders, and separately for stabilizer encoders, stabilizer decoders or both.

For a stabilizer code everything is decided by linear algebra over the field with \(d\) elements. Given a set \(E\) of erased positions, some operators supported on \(E\) commute with all stabilizers; some of these are stabilizers themselves and harmless. The quotient counts the logical operations that the erasure leaves undecided, \(d^{a(E)}\) of them. The paper proves that syndrome correction, which guesses one of them, has conditional fidelity \(d^{-a(E)}\), and that no quantum operation on the surviving systems can do better. The optimal error of the code is therefore the average of \(1-d^{-a(E)}\) over erasure patterns.

The lower bound on the exponent averages over random stabilizer codes. A fixed operator is an undetectable logical operator with probability at most \(d^{-(n-k)}\), and there are \(d^{2|E|}\) operators on the erased set. Hence a pattern is uncorrectable with probability at most \(d^{2|E|-(n-k)}\), which is small until \(|E|\) approaches \((n-k)/2\). The exponent is the cheapest compromise between erasing many systems and being unlucky with the code. Above the critical rate the cheapest way to fail is simply to erase the fraction \((1-r)/2\).

The upper bound uses no structure of the code. For an erasure probability \(p'\) slightly above \((1-r)/2\) the rate exceeds capacity, so a known result says that the error stays bounded away from zero. The same encoder and decoder at the true probability \(p\) face the same patterns, only with other probabilities, and patterns with a fraction \(p'\) of erasures are exponentially rarer by the binary relative entropy. This transfers the constant error at \(p'\) into an exponentially small but unavoidable error at \(p\).

Below the critical rate the random code is limited by a few bad codes. Discarding codes with logical operators of low weight improves the exponent at low rates; for \(d=2\), \(p=0.01\) and \(r=0.1\) our evaluation gives 0.751 after expurgation against 0.594 for random coding and 1.390 for the upper bound. Two related tasks, guessing the physical error and classical communication without feedback, share the exponent above the critical rate at corresponding parameters. Closing the gap at low rates is the open problem.

methods.technique: Optimal erasure recovery from a count of undecided logical operators
methods.explanation: The fidelity of a stabilizer code after an erasure is computed exactly, both for syndrome correction and for the best conceivable recovery. The first follows from a count inside one coset. The second follows from Bessel's inequality applied to the Kraus operators of the recovery.
math: Replace the erased systems by maximally mixed ones. This is the same as applying a uniformly random Pauli (Weyl) operator with support in \(E\). Let \(\mathsf S\) be the stabilizer labels, \(\mathsf S^\perp\) the labels commuting with them, and \(V_E\) the labels supported on \(E\). Put \[K_E=\mathsf S^\perp\cap V_E,\qquad H_E=\mathsf S\cap V_E,\qquad a(E)=\dim K_E-\dim H_E.\] Given a syndrome, the error is uniform over a coset of \(K_E\). A correction succeeds exactly on one coset of \(H_E\), so the success probability is \(|H_E|/|K_E|=d^{-a(E)}\) for every rule that matches the syndrome.

For an arbitrary recovery, the channel seen by the logical state in one syndrome sector is the uniform mixture of the \(d^{a(E)}\) distinct logical operators \(\overline W_g\). Let \(Q_j\) be the Kraus operators of the recovery restricted to that sector and \(M=d^k\). The operators \(\overline W_g^\dagger/\sqrt M\) are orthonormal, so \[F=\frac{1}{d^{a}M}\sum_{j,g}\Bigl|\Bigl\langle\tfrac{\overline W_g^\dagger}{\sqrt M},Q_j\Bigr\rangle\Bigr|^2\le\frac1{d^{a}M}\sum_j\operatorname{tr}Q_j^\dagger Q_j=d^{-a(E)}.\] Syndrome correction attains the bound. Optimising over general recoveries therefore gains nothing for a stabilizer encoder.

The error and the probability of an uncorrectable pattern have the same exponent, because \((1-d^{-1})\,\mathbf 1[a>0]\le1-d^{-a}\le\mathbf 1[a>0]\). A symmetry that we checked on the five-qubit code (editorial): for complementary sets \(a(E)+a(\bar E)=2k\), which is the cleaning lemma. A pattern is fully correctable exactly when the erased side holds no information about the logical state.
methods.transfer: The Bessel argument bounds the recovery fidelity for any noise that acts as a mixture of orthogonal logical unitaries within classical sectors, such as Pauli noise with side information or detected leakage. The count of undecided logical operators is also the quantity to compute when comparing codes under atom loss, since it needs only ranks over a finite field.

methods.technique: Error exponents by changing the erasure probability
methods.explanation: Both directions compare the true channel with the one at which the rate would sit at capacity. The random-coding bound finds the cheapest failure by minimising over the erased fraction, and the converse shows by a change of measure that no code can avoid the failure at the capacity fraction.
math: Write \(D(t\|p)=t\ln\tfrac tp+(1-t)\ln\tfrac{1-t}{1-p}\). The number of erasures is binomial, and averaging the bound for random codes gives the exponent \[E_{\rm rc}=\min_{0\le t\le1}\bigl\{D(t\|p)+(1-r-2t)_+\ln d\bigr\}.\] For \(t<(1-r)/2\) the derivative of the bracket is \(\ln\frac{t(1-p)}{p(1-t)}-2\ln d\), which vanishes at \(\tau=d^2p/(1-p+d^2p)\).

If \(\tau\ge(1-r)/2\), that is \(r\ge1-2\tau=r_{\rm crit}\), the minimum sits at the corner \(t=(1-r)/2\) and \[E_{\rm rc}=D\bigl(\tfrac{1-r}2\,\big\|\,p\bigr).\] Otherwise \(E_{\rm rc}=(1-r)\ln d-\ln(1-p+d^2p)\).

For the converse take any sequence of codes with rate at least \(r\), and let \(p'>(1-r)/2\) be an erasure probability at which their error stays above a constant \(c\). Patterns whose erased fraction is within \(\delta\) of \(p'\) carry error at least \(c/2\) for large \(n\). On those patterns the ratio of probabilities at \(p\) and at \(p'\) is at least \(\exp[-n(D(p'\|p)+\delta C)]\), where \(C\) is a constant, so \[\varepsilon_n(p)\ \ge\ \tfrac c2\,e^{-n(D(p'\|p)+\delta C)}.\] Letting \(\delta\to0\) and \(p'\to(1-r)/2\) shows that the exponent is at most \(D(\tfrac{1-r}2\|p)\) for every code and decoder.
methods.transfer: The argument works for any channel that is a mixture, with known label, of channels that do not depend on the parameter: the code is fixed and only the weights change. It converts a strong enough statement above capacity into an exponent below it. For noise whose components cannot be read by the receiver, the label is hidden and the argument needs a quantum change of measure, which is where exact exponents are still missing.
